title: Session surge cheatstrip - microbench notes and quick comparison
content:
Quick note: doing a compact, operationally-oriented microbenchmark comparing three operational patterns we keep suggesting in docs:

1) Always-hot session (reserved slot, persistent KV cache)
2) On-demand session (cold start, fast warmup via prefetch)
3) Opportunistic-batch session (short lived, aggregated batching)

Purpose: produce a short, readable artifact we can paste into the console help UI and the internal playbook. Not a full paper — more of a cheatstrip for engs/SEs when choosing routing/burst knobs.

Setup (short):
- Model: openbase-7B-quant (int4-ish runtime build) — representative SFT-style chat backbone
- HW: H100-80GB (dev cluster node type emulated); slotized runtime with slot size 64 tokens
- Workload: sessionized chat sequences, 1–8 turns, median turn length 40 tokens
- Traffic shapes: sustained (QPS steady 20), short surge (40qps for 30s every 5m), microburst (100 qps for 10s)
- Warm states: hot (KV primed), cold (fresh process), prefetched (KV keys for likely prefix only)
- Measurement windows: 30m sustained, 10 repeats for surge/microburst with 95% CI reported roughly

What we measured:
- p50/p90/p95/p99 for response latency (end-to-end two-phase: request + generation)
- tail-penalty (p99 - p50) as a quick indicator of jitter
- quick cost proxy: amortized GPU-ms per completed response (GPU-time * spot hour $ / 3600), rough unit cents-per-query (CPQ) at these shapes

Compact results (text table). Numbers are illustrative from the bench run on 2028-03-10 (dev cluster).

| Pattern                 | p50 (ms) | p90 (ms) | p95 (ms) | p99 (ms) | tail-penalty (ms) | cost proxy (cents/query) | notes |
|------------------------|----------:|---------:|---------:|---------:|------------------:|-------------------------:|-------|
| Always-hot (primed KV) |     58    |    85    |   110    |   180    |               122  |                    0.26   | best steady latency, low variance
| On-demand (cold)       |    210    |   480    |   700    |  1300    |              1090  |                    0.42   | cold penalty visible, spikes during warmup
| Prefetch (partial KV)  |     90    |   140    |   190    |   250    |               160  |                    0.30   | good compromise, faster than cold for first turn
| Opportunistic-batch    |     85    |   170    |   240    |   520    |               435  |                    0.20   | lower cost at throughput, higher tail under microbursts

Quick textual charts (ascii bars — scaled to p90). Each bar units approximate relative magnitude of p90 latency.
- Always-hot  : [#####       ] 85ms
- Prefetch    : [########    ] 140ms
- Opportunistic: [############] 170ms
- On-demand    : [############################] 480ms

Burst sensitivity (observations):
- Microbursts (100 qps x 10s): opportunistic-batch saw p99 blow up to 1.2s when the scheduler hit slab contention; prefetch and always-hot held better but p95 worsened ~1.6x.
- Short surge (40 qps x 30s): on-demand mode showed consistent warmup spikes for the first 45s of the surge window; cost increases due to higher GPU-ms per completed response because of repeated cold starts.
- Sustained: always-hot is the cheapest per-response when utilization >60% of reserved slot; opportunistic batched is cheaper when mean utilization <40% but you pay with tail.

Cost vs latency tradeoffs (hand-rail takeaways):
- If customer SLO is p95 < 250ms: recommend reserved/pinned sessions w/ hot KV or prefetching for first-turn priming. (cost: moderate but predictable)
- If customer prioritizes minimum cost and can tolerate p99 up to ~500ms: opportunistic batching with burst smoothing works well for long-tailed low-utilization tenants.
- If traffic is highly spiky and unpredictable: hybrid policy — route to hot pool first, fallback to opportunistic when hot pools are saturated; add quick-prefetch on cold path to reduce first-turn hit.

Open operational notes (to-do / unresolved):
- We need a short script to surface these CPQ numbers automatically in the console for a given customer profile (ticket: JIRA-PE-4721).
- How sensitive are the prefetched keys to model & prompt style? I saw variance when using long-system-prompts vs short ones — we should run a small ablation.
- Opportunistic batching scheduler currently uses a 15ms hold window; need a sweep on hold-window vs tail for microburst shapes.

Short checklist for console copy (what to include in the UI):
- 1-sentence: "Reserved hot sessions = predictable low-latency; batching = cost-efficient at the expense of tail."
- Short table (p50/p95/p99 + cost proxy) for three recommended presets: hot, prefetch, batch.
- Short explainer: "When to use each" with practical thresholds (QPS sustain > X, burst > Y).

Notes to self (rough):
- This doc intentionally compact. If we like, expand to longer notebook showing event traces.
- Add a tiny visual (sparklines) for p95 time series for each shape — console can render it as small chart.

Appendix: quick micro-numbers (raw sample for one run, first-turn only)
- Always-hot: mean GPU-ms per response 34ms, 95% GPU-ms 68ms
- Prefetch: mean GPU-ms 39ms, 95% GPU-ms 84ms
- Opportunistic: mean GPU-ms 28ms, 95% GPU-ms 120ms (variance from queueing)
- Cold/on-demand: mean GPU-ms 52ms, 95% GPU-ms 240ms (includes startup overhead)

Slack refs / threads: #runtime-bench (see thread pinned March 11), will paste log link once sanitized.

Decision bits:
- For console quick-help, use the three-row mini-table (hot/prefetch/opportunistic) + one-sentence guidance. Keep this doc as canonical short source.

If anyone wants the raw bench harness and CSVs, DM me (Asha) and I will sanitize/remove internal hostnames.
